clone_cost.note: our estimate with assumptions visible; not a claim about the team

assumptions: a wiki or knowledge base with a review workflow you can post diffs into (MediaWiki pending changes, or a PR-style flow)
a per-claim research budget, since a pass costs a search plus several model calls for every claim on the page
a decision about contested facts: staff the disagreement bucket, or suppress that category rather than flood maintainers
value.estimate: 2-3 weeks — the ledger is the project, the model calls are glue
value.why: The walkthrough is ordinary orchestration over two APIs: extract, prioritise, research, judge, draft, cross-check, render a diff. What takes the time is the claim ledger — extracting claims reliably, keying them so a re-run recognises the same claim in a re-edited article, and the due-date and link graph on top — plus the fixture recorder that keeps iteration cheap. The dependency-free core design is what makes the second part cheap to get right.

data_and_models.value: Two vendor APIs with explicit division of labour: Parallel for web research, Gemini for the judgement (still true / changed / sources disagree). Between them a dependency-free Python ledger tracking each claim, its last-checked time, its next due time and its links to other claims; vendor SDKs only at the edges. Stateless service on Cloud Run scaled to zero; the Built With list adds Firestore and pymongo for storage. No model is trained and no accuracy figure is given for either the judge or the researcher.

how_it_works.value: Python backend, plain JavaScript frontend with no framework and no build step, one Cloud Run service that scales to zero. Parallel does the research, Gemini does the judging. The part the author spent the most time on is the ledger: a small dependency-free Python core that tracks every claim, when it was last checked, when it is due next and what else it is connected to. It never touches the network, so the interesting logic is testable without a cloud account or an API key, and the vendor SDKs live only at the edges. Built With additionally names FastAPI, uvicorn, Firestore, pymongo, Docker, Cloud Build and Secret Manager.

how_they_tested.value: A real harness discipline is described rather than measured: the first live run recorded every search result and model response to disk so all later development replayed from fixtures at zero cost, and the ledger core has no dependencies, so most of the test suite runs on a bare Python interpreter with no database, emulator or cloud project. No case count, coverage figure or pass rate is published, there is no evaluation of the judge's accuracy against labelled facts, and no repository is linked, so none of it can be inspected.

limits_they_disclosed.value: Cost. One pass over a single page is a web search per claim plus several Gemini calls, which is fine once and not fine while tuning a prompt forty times in an afternoon. The answer was to record fixtures: the first live run wrote every search result and model response to disk, after which the whole pipeline could replay from them for free — so the classify stage could be rewritten and all stages run end to end at no cost. The same reasoning drove the local-first design: the ledger core has no dependencies at all, so most of the test suite runs on a bare Python interpreter with nothing installed, and the billing meter did not start until the day of deployment.

value.relation: the same shape — a machine ranking facts for a human to act on, deliberately stopping short of acting — and the two pages differ almost entirely on whether the judgement is checkable: Continuity returns old text, new text, a citation and a confidence score per claim, while the fisheries tool returns a risk classification whose own page says there is no ground truth for it.

both convert an unverifiable judgement into an artifact a person can check (a cited diff, a signed finding) and both keep the human as the writer of record; the difference is what they attach evidence to — one grounds a claim against the live web on a schedule, the other against a versioned rule set in CI.

both are staged agent pipelines that publish a dollar figure, and read together they move the number worth tracking: Greenlight quotes cost per run against a measured output, Continuity quotes total build cost and explains that fixtures made every later iteration free — so iteration cost, not run cost, is what decides whether a pipeline is developable.

what_breaks_first.value: The fixed staleness window. 'Skip what was verified last week' is a single guess about decay rates applied uniformly, and it is wrong in both directions for the facts this targets: a film's release date almost never moves, while 'current holder of X' can move in a day — so the budget is spent re-checking stable facts while the volatile ones age out between passes. Second: the reviewer's queue. 'Sources disagree' is a terminal category with no triage described, and on a long contested article it can hold a large share of the claims; a maintainer handed forty cited diffs and thirty unresolved disagreements has been given a new job, not a lighter one.

what_it_does.value: One button on an article page; no setup, config or schedule to configure. The agent reads the page, writes down every factual claim it makes one at a time, decides which are worth checking now (claims verified last week are skipped), researches each on the live web through Parallel, judges what came back with Gemini as still-true, changed or sources-disagree, drafts the edit with the citation attached, cross-checks that edit against the rest of the page so one fixed paragraph cannot contradict another, and hands it back as a diff with old text, new text, sources and a confidence score. Then it stops and waits: approve, rewrite or throw out — nothing reaches the page until a person says so.

what_it_is.value: A MediaWiki companion that re-reads a page fact by fact on a schedule, researches each claim against the live web, and hands the maintainer a cited diff for every fact that quietly stopped being true — never writing to the article itself.

what_to_steal.value: Record fixtures on the first live run — write every search result and model response to disk once, and every later iteration is free; that single habit is what made the whole thing developable on a hackathon budget. Keep vendor SDKs at the edges around a dependency-free core so the interesting logic runs on a bare interpreter with no key. Schedule re-verification per claim with a last-checked and next-due time rather than per page, and keep a link graph between claims so an edit to one paragraph can be checked against its neighbours. And always hand back a diff with citations instead of writing to the system of record.

continuity-g7bty0.name: Continuity
verdict_reasons: soundness 0.50 over 64% of the rubric; 0 named unknown(s) remain → publishable with caveats
continuity-g7bty0.worth_note: The diagnosis is worth more than the demo: a fact that used to be true and quietly stopped being true looks exactly like every correct sentence around it, and nobody edited the page — the world moved on. Treating wiki rot as a decay problem with a per-claim due date instead of an error problem is the right shape, and keeping the human as writer of record (a cited diff, never a publish) is the right posture for public knowledge infrastructure. The write-up also documents its own development discipline in the same breath as the product, which lets a reader check the cost claim against the fixture claim.

data_and_models.value: No model; a rule/classification engine over fixtures it generates itself. Nothing in the capture describes where the twelve vector definitions came from or how a missed vector would be discovered.

how_it_works.value: 100% Rust. Engine logic in src/cvm.rs and src/main.rs; src/bin/gen_fixtures.rs generates clean and malicious fixtures; tests/simulation_matrix.rs runs the twelve scenarios; .github/workflows/test.yml provisions a runner, caches dependencies, compiles and executes the whole suite per change.

how_they_tested.value: A real harness is described - a fixture generator plus a twelve-scenario matrix executed by CI on every commit - which is the right shape for this kind of validator. But the page links no repository, workflow or run id, so the green-checkmark claim cannot be checked, and a suite whose cases and fixtures are both authored by the system measures agreement with itself.

limits_they_disclosed.value: The whole framework was written and committed from a mobile device, so every pushed command had to work first time; runner compilation and dependency conflicts were the failure mode to avoid.

what_to_steal.value: gen_fixtures.rs as a test *generator*: emit the clean and adversarial cases from the same spec the validator consumes, then let CI rebuild the whole matrix on every commit. It makes a regression impossible to hide and costs one file.
